title: Are we being told truth about cyber-disasters?
summary: When it comes to recent tech outages, there have been a lot of coincidences. Some would say too many. The US grounded all departing flights — for only the second time since the September 11 attacks 25 years ago. Microsoft, the linchpin of the entire English legal system, was down for nearly 24 hours, weeks after the company announced 60,000 job cuts. And earlier this week, several American banks were down. Back in the UK, the National Grid has had to publicly deny an online hoax claiming that the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 will trigger power outages tomorrow. Then there was the brief Apple outage on Tuesday, and the National Security Agency’s temporary outage on its internal network. One cyber insider told me it’s all a bit like “the old stories about UFOs. If a big report comes out, then it’s worth running all the stories, and suddenly there appear to be loads of problems. The baseline number of reports hasn’t changed. What has changed is the newsworthiness threshold”. But that isn’t all that has changed. The American public’s wafer-thin tolerance for being asked to prepare for danger and then be told there isn’t any seems to have snapped. Even Karoline Leavitt, once a loyal press secretary to Donald Trump’s White House, told Fox News that the government should come clean on tech outages, adding that “transparency is key”. When the public doesn’t believe what the state is telling them, that is obviously bad. This spate of significant outages has taken out much of our increasingly digitally dependent way of life — and whether it’s Russia, Iran or a cleaner unplugging a key socket to do the hoovering, everything feels distinctly leery. In the UK, the haze of Covid lingers in the air. Economic pressures and uncertainty from the USA emphasise this yet further — and then there’s the fact that both MI5 and GCHQ have been very plainly telling us to take cybersecurity seriously and get our houses in order. However much company comms departments may trill that everything’s fine and there have been zero cyberattacks, it’s extremely clear that everything is very much not fine, although it may have become our new normal — not helped by Silicon Valley reporting that their every brilliant, beautiful new toy will either kill us or replace us, but that we should definitely use it every day and pay for the privilege. And back here, more than one person I have spoken to feels distinctly gaslit by this cycle of being “nudged” by government advice into anxious prepping,…
